reasoning: The broad problem — that LLM-judge reliability varies across task domains and that "no judge is uniformly robust" across tasks — is well documented (e.g. "Judge Reliability Harness", arXiv 2603.05399; "LLMs Cannot Reliably Judge (Yet?)", 2506.09443; the LLM-as-a-Judge surveys), and IRT-based work (2602.00521) already separates latent judge ability from item difficulty. However, none of these works frames or tests the specific hypothesis in the proposal: whether an individual judge's per-item oversight failure is a stable CROSS-DOMAIN trait — i.e. computing difficulty-controlled pairwise correlation of per-item failures across matched hard-ground-truth binary items in arithmetic/code/factual-QA and outputting a per-judge domain-transfer matrix. Existing work reports aggregate per-domain accuracy heterogeneity and within-domain perturbation robustness, but the difficulty-controlled item-level cross-domain correlation framing (predicting failure on code from failure on math) is unexplored, placing this in the partially_addressed band. Confidence is moderate because the IRT and harness literatures are close enough that an unread paper could contain this analysis as a sub-result.

evidence.title: Judge Reliability Harness: Stress Testing the Reliability of LLM Judges
evidence.summary: Evaluates LLM judges across multiple benchmarks (writing, misuse, safety, agentic) finding no judge uniformly robust and that robustness is highly task-dependent. Studies within-domain perturbation robustness, NOT cross-domain correlation of per-item failures controlling for difficulty — confirmed via WebFetch that it does not build per-judge cross-domain transfer matrices.

evidence.title: Diagnosing the Reliability of LLM-as-a-Judge via Item Response Theory
evidence.summary: Uses IRT to separate latent judge ability from item difficulty — directly relevant to the proposal's difficulty-controlling goal. But its framing estimates judge ability/reliability; abstract and structure give no indication it tests whether that ability is stable/transferable across distinct task domains (math vs code vs QA), which is the proposal's core question.

evidence.title: LLMs Cannot Reliably Judge (Yet?): A Comprehensive Assessment on the Robustness of LLM-as-a-Judge
evidence.summary: Documents that judges are inconsistent and that no judge is uniformly reliable across tasks, establishing the domain-specificity premise but not the item-level cross-domain failure-correlation analysis.

evidence.title: On scalable oversight with weak LLMs judging strong LLMs
evidence.summary: Core scalable-oversight motivation: weak/cheap judges overseeing stronger models, reliability varying by task. Provides the safety framing but does not study whether judge failure is a cross-domain trait.

evidence.title: From Calculation to Adjudication: Examining LLM judges on Mathematical Reasoning Tasks
evidence.summary: Studies LLM judges specifically on math reasoning with hard ground truth and pairwise correct/incorrect candidate judgments — methodologically similar to one domain of the proposal, but single-domain only, with no cross-domain transfer comparison.

evidence.title: Diagnosing LLM Judge Reliability: Conformal Prediction Sets and Transitivity Violations
evidence.summary: Another judge-reliability diagnostic line (conformal/transitivity) showing active interest in characterizing judge failure structure, but focused on logical consistency rather than cross-domain per-item failure correlation.
